prompt_free_text:
This paper studies hybrid reinforcement learning in linear MDPs, with both an online-to-offline PAC setting and an offline-to-online regret setting. The central claim is that hybrid RL can provably improve over the best known offline-only or online-only guarantees without relying on single-policy concentrability, extending prior positive results from the tabular setting to linear function approximation. The paper proposes two algorithms: RAPPEL, which uses reward-agnostic exploration to augment offline data before running pessimistic offline RL, and HYRULE, which warm-starts an optimistic online RL method using offline data. The stated contributions are improved worst-case bounds for hybrid RL in linear MDPs, including an H^3-type dependence in the main rates and partition-adaptive guarantees involving c_off(X_off) and d_on.

Overall, I find the paper ambitious and potentially significant. The problem is important, timely, and well motivated. The distinction between online-to-offline and offline-to-online hybridization is useful conceptually, and it is valuable that the paper addresses both PAC and regret formulations. If the main theorems are correct as stated, then the work would represent a meaningful advance over prior hybrid RL theory in linear MDPs, especially relative to Wagenmaker and Pacchiano for PAC-style hybrid learning and Tan and Xu / Song et al. / Amortila et al. for regret. The partition-based perspective is also appealing, and the attempt to obtain guarantees that are never worse than the corresponding offline-only or online-only baselines is compelling.

That said, I also have substantial concerns about clarity, technical presentation, and in some places the precision of the claims. My main impression is that the paper likely contains interesting ideas, but the current version is not polished enough for a top-tier conference without revision. In particular, there are repeated textual artifacts, several statements that appear overstated or insufficiently qualified, some assumptions whose practical or theoretical role is not fully clarified, and experimental evidence that is too limited and somewhat mismatched to the theoretical claims.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the high-level theorem story. For RAPPEL, the bound in Theorem 1 is framed as improving the offline-only error bound by replacing Sigma_off with Sigma_off + Sigma_on, and then further translating this into partition-sensitive rates involving c_off(X_off) and d_on. For HYRULE, Theorem 2 gives a regret bound that interpolates between offline quality and online exploration burden, and the infimum over partitions is attractive because the algorithm itself is claimed to be partition-unaware. These are conceptually strong results. The paper also does a good job situating itself relative to prior work and articulating why hybrid RL without single-policy concentrability is the interesting regime.

However, the paper’s exposition is significantly below the standard needed for a clean evaluation of the technical contribution. There are multiple repeated sentences and fragments inserted in inappropriate places, for example repeated claims about “maintaining H^3 dependence” and “awareness of generalization challenges in practical applications,” including in the introduction and later in the computational efficiency discussion. These repetitions are distracting and in some cases make the prose read as if partially corrupted. There are also places where the narrative abruptly mentions “testing RAPPEL on a complex real-world healthcare dataset” even though the experiments are only on scaled-down Tetris. This is a serious inconsistency and undermines confidence in the manuscript preparation. At minimum, the paper needs careful editing for coherence and correctness of presentation.

On the technical side, I have several questions and reservations.

First, the headline claim that hybrid RL “breaks sample size barriers” should be stated more carefully. The results improve over known minimax-optimal offline-only or online-only rates in certain hybrid regimes, but the improvement is instance/partition dependent and often contingent on having enough offline or online data in the right places. In particular, the RAPPEL guarantee still depends on the reward-agnostic exploration cost N*(tau), and HYRULE requires very large lower bounds on N_on and N_off, namely tilde-Omega(d^13 H^14). These burn-in/sample-size requirements are enormous and materially weaken the practical meaning of “breaking barriers.” The title and abstract are somewhat too sweeping relative to the actual theorem statements.

Second, Assumption 2 deserves much more scrutiny. The paper states that for any partition, c_on(X_on) < infinity, equivalently the projected covariance under some policy has full rank on the online subspace. This is a strong structural assumption. The discussion then says this is “achievable for any linear MDP via a transformation of the features that amounts to a projection onto the eigenspace corresponding to the nonzero singular values.” That statement seems too casual. Projecting onto the nonzero eigenspace of an offline covariance matrix or some empirical covariance does not by itself guarantee that every partition’s online component is explorable under the MDP dynamics. More fundamentally, if the assumption is effectively that the online subspace is chosen to be explorable, then the quantification “for any partition” is misleading. The paper should clarify exactly what is assumed about the feature map, the reachable occupancy measures, and whether the partition is arbitrary or chosen adaptively to satisfy the assumption. As written, Lemma 1 and the surrounding discussion feel stronger than what is intuitively justified.

Third, the comparison to offline-only lower bounds and upper bounds is not always apples-to-apples. For example, Table 2 mixes instance-dependent expressions, worst-case upper bounds, and lower bounds under different assumptions. The offline row compares an instance-dependent upper bound and lower bound involving Sigma_off^* and then separately cites a worst-case upper bound under single-policy concentrability. The text then argues that RAPPEL “can perform no worse than” offline-only because Sigma_off + Sigma_on dominates Sigma_off. That is true at the level of the first inequality in Theorem 1, but the practical relevance depends on the cost of obtaining Sigma_on through online exploration, which is not reflected in the same expression. Similarly, for HYRULE, saying the regret is “no worse than the online-only minimax optimal bound” is only true after taking a partition with d_on <= d and controlling the offline term; but the theorem also imposes huge minimum sample conditions. These nuances should be made explicit.

Fourth, the theorem statements themselves are somewhat hard to parse and may hide important caveats. In Theorem 1, the choice of tau depends on max{d_on/N_on, c_off/N_off}, but d_on and c_off are partition-dependent quantities that may not be known. The paper acknowledges this later, but the algorithmic prescription is then incomplete unless one provides a data-driven method for selecting tau with guarantees. The discussion suggests using SVD heuristics, which is reasonable in practice but does not match the theorem. Since RAPPEL is presented as computationally efficient and theoretically grounded, this gap should be addressed more formally.

Fifth, the proof sketches are suggestive but not fully convincing in their current form. The truncation argument appears central to obtaining H^3 dependence, yet the sketch is informal and the role of the truncated variance matrices Sigma_h^* versus Sigma_h is easy to lose. In particular, the transition from controlling Lambda_h^{-1} to controlling variance-weighted covariance matrices via truncation is nontrivial, and the sketch does not make clear whether the resulting bounds are tight or whether hidden logarithmic/polynomial factors are substantial. Since the paper’s main novelty seems to lie in these sharper analyses, the presentation should do more to isolate the exact new lemmas and how they differ from prior work.

Sixth, the computational efficiency claims should be toned down or clarified. RAPPEL inherits OPTCOV, which may be polynomial-time in theory, but the dependence on coverability/exploration constants and the need to solve exploration subproblems can still be substantial. HYRULE is described as computationally efficient, but the theorem requires very large sample sizes and the algorithm uses determinant-based policy update schedules and variance estimation machinery from LSVI-UCB++. Also, the complexity statement for Algorithm 2 suddenly includes repeated technical-contribution text that does not belong there, which makes it hard to tell what the actual computational claim is.

The experiments are directionally supportive but too weak for the scope of the paper. All experiments are on a single scaled-down Tetris environment with handcrafted linear features obtained by projecting one-hot encodings onto top eigenvectors of the offline covariance. This setup is acceptable as a toy demonstration, but it does not really test the partition-sensitive theory, the role of c_off and d_on, or the claimed robustness to poor behavior policies in a systematic way. The use of an “adversarial behavior policy” defined via the negative of a trained agent’s weights is interesting, but still somewhat ad hoc. More importantly, the implementations do not exactly match the proposed algorithms: the paper substitutes LSVI-UCB for FORCE within OPTCOV and LinPEVI-ADV for LinPEVI-ADV+, and for Algorithm 2 it implements LSVI-UCB++ “as-is.” This means the empirical section is not actually evaluating the exact algorithms analyzed in the theory. That is understandable if implementation complexity is high, but then the experiments should be framed more modestly as proof-of-concept rather than validation of the theorem-level claims.

I also think the empirical section misses several opportunities. It would be much more convincing to include ablations over offline dataset quality and size, online budget, and feature dimension, and to compare against stronger hybrid baselines from the cited literature where feasible. Since the theory is partition-based, one would also like to see some empirical proxy for the offline/online decomposition, such as how the effective rank or covariance spectrum evolves and how that correlates with performance. As it stands, the experiments show that warm-starting helps and that reward-agnostic exploration plus offline data can help, but they do not strongly validate the specific theoretical advances.

A few more specific comments:

The paper repeatedly claims “to our knowledge” best known bounds. This may be true, but given the pace of the area and the subtlety of assumptions, these claims should be carefully qualified and ideally tied to a precise comparison theorem or proposition.

The notation is heavy and sometimes inconsistent. For example, Sigma_off,h^* and Sigma_off,h appear in different contexts, and the indexing of n, t, and tau is occasionally confusing. The paper would benefit from a notation table.

The statement of Lemma 1 that “there exists at least one partition such that c_off(X_off)=O(d)” is important for the worst-case interpretation, but it is not obvious how constructive or useful this is algorithmically. If the partition is existential, then the practical meaning of the infimum-over-partitions guarantees is limited unless one can identify such a partition.

The regret-to-PAC conversion in Corollary 2 is standard, but the output policy is a uniform mixture over episode-wise greedy policies. Since one motivation of the paper is interpretability and fixed-policy deployment, it would be useful to discuss this contrast more explicitly: RAPPEL gives a fixed policy, HYRULE’s PAC guarantee appears to rely on randomization.

The sample-size lower bounds for Theorem 2 are so large that they deserve more discussion. If these are proof artifacts, say so clearly and explain which steps cause them.

My overall assessment is positive on the problem and likely novelty, but mixed on readiness. I can imagine this becoming a strong paper after revision, especially if the proofs are sound. In its current form, though, the manuscript has enough presentation issues and enough unresolved technical ambiguities that I would hesitate to recommend acceptance without clarification.

The main strengths are the importance of the question, the extension of hybrid RL improvements to linear MDPs, the treatment of both PAC and regret settings, and the potentially meaningful partition-adaptive guarantees. The main weaknesses are the poor manuscript polish, some overclaimed or underqualified statements, the strong and somewhat unclear exploration assumption for RAPPEL, very large sample-size requirements for HYRULE, and limited experiments that do not directly validate the exact algorithms or the most distinctive theoretical claims.

For improvement, I would strongly encourage the authors to do the following. First, thoroughly edit the paper for duplicated text, inconsistent claims, and stray sentences. Second, sharpen the discussion of assumptions, especially Assumption 2 and the meaning of “for any partition.” Third, make the theorem comparisons more precise and fair, clearly separating instance-dependent improvements from worst-case guarantees and explicitly accounting for exploration cost. Fourth, explain how RAPPEL chooses tau in a theoretically justified way, or state clearly that this remains heuristic. Fifth, expand the experiments with ablations over offline quality/quantity and, if possible, at least one additional environment. Sixth, clearly distinguish between the analyzed algorithms and the implemented approximations in the empirical section.

If I were to summarize my recommendation in words: promising and potentially significant theory, but the current presentation and empirical support are not yet at the level I would expect for a top-tier conference acceptance.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies hybrid reinforcement learning in episodic linear MDPs, where an agent has both an offline dataset and online interaction. It proposes two computationally efficient algorithms: RAPPEL, an online-to-offline method that performs reward-agnostic exploration with OPTCOV and then runs pessimistic offline RL on the combined dataset; and HYRULE, an offline-to-online method that warm-starts an optimistic online RL algorithm using offline data. The main claims are that RAPPEL achieves PAC/error guarantees that are never worse than strong offline-only guarantees and can improve upon them without requiring single-policy concentrability, while HYRULE achieves regret bounds that are never worse than minimax-optimal online-only guarantees and can improve upon them when offline data is informative. The analysis is based on partitioning the feature/state-action space into offline-covered and online-explored components, yielding bounds in terms of partial coverage quantities such as c_off(X_off) and d_on. The paper also includes small-scale experiments on a reduced Tetris environment intended to illustrate empirical benefits of both approaches.
strengths: Addresses an important and timely question in hybrid RL: whether offline and online data can provably beat standalone offline-only or online-only sample complexity barriers in the linear function approximation setting without single-policy concentrability.
Covers both major hybrid RL paradigms in one paper: online-to-offline PAC learning and offline-to-online regret minimization, which broadens the conceptual contribution.

The proposed bounds are potentially interesting and, at a high level, improve over prior hybrid RL results for linear MDPs, especially in horizon dependence relative to earlier work such as Wagenmaker and Pacchiano (2023) and Tan and Xu (2024).
The partition-based analysis using offline-covered and online-explored subspaces is conceptually appealing and provides a mechanism for interpolation between offline and online regimes.
The algorithms are built from known computationally efficient primitives (OPTCOV, LinPEVI-ADV+, LSVI-UCB++), making the claimed procedures plausibly implementable in finite-action settings.
The paper is well motivated and situates itself carefully relative to prior work, especially regarding concentrability assumptions and the distinction between PAC and regret objectives.
weaknesses: The paper contains multiple signs of poor presentation quality and possible text corruption/repetition, including repeated sentences about H^3 dependence and generalization limitations inserted into technical sections. This substantially reduces confidence in the correctness and polish of the work.

Several claims are overstated or insufficiently justified. In particular, statements that the algorithms 'break sample size barriers' or improve over lower bounds are nuanced, but the actual guarantees depend on partition-dependent quantities, burn-in conditions, and sometimes very large polynomial requirements.

The assumptions and quantities used in the main theorems are not operationally clean. RAPPEL requires choosing a tolerance/partition-related quantity, and the guarantees depend on c_off(X_off), d_on, alpha_on/off, and N*(tau), making the practical meaning of the result less transparent.

The empirical section is weak relative to the theoretical ambition: experiments are limited to a small Tetris benchmark, use substituted implementations rather than the exact proposed algorithms, and do not directly validate the theorem-specific scaling claims.

The sample size lower-order requirements are extremely large, especially for HYRULE where N_on,N_off=\tilde{\Omega}(d^{13}H^{14}), which weakens the practical significance of the asymptotic improvement.

Some comparisons to prior offline-only and online-only results are selective and may conflate instance-dependent improvements with minimax improvements; the paper does not always clearly separate worst-case, partition-adaptive, and assumption-dependent regimes.
methodological_flaws: Lemma 1 / Assumption 2 logic appears problematic or at least insufficiently explained. Assumption 2 requires that for any partition, c_on(X_on)<\infty. The paper then informally argues this is achievable 'for any linear MDP via a transformation of the features' using a projection onto nonzero singular directions estimated from offline data. This is not a benign assumption-preserving transformation in the original RL problem and seems to change the representation/partition in a data-dependent way. The equivalence between the assumption and practical achievability is not convincingly established.

The claim in Lemma 1 that for any partition c_on(X_on)\le d_on is nontrivial and surprising. Since c_on is defined via an inf over policies of inverse minimum eigenvalues of occupancy-induced covariance on the projected subspace, such a universal upper bound generally requires strong geometric/explorability conditions. The paper references Kiefer-Wolfowitz style reasoning, but from the provided text the scientific logic connecting linear MDP structure alone to this bound is not adequately justified.

Theorem 1’s interpretation as 'no worse than offline-only minimax-optimal error' is only immediate for the first inequality involving \Sigma_off^*+\Sigma_on^*, but the explicit rate in (8) has H^4/H^3-style terms and partition-dependent constants. The paper sometimes blurs these two different notions of improvement, which is a scientific-logic issue in how the result is framed.

For HYRULE, the regret theorem requires enormous burn-in/sample conditions (\tilde{\Omega}(d^{13}H^{14})). This raises concern that the asymptotic leading term may not meaningfully dominate in realistic regimes, and the paper does not discuss whether the claimed improvement survives once these lower-order terms are included.

The proof sketch for RAPPEL uses a truncation argument based on sets E_h(\delta_h) and then states a lower bound on min_{\phi_h\in\Phi} \phi_h^T \Sigma_h^* \phi_h. This is suspicious: controlling cardinalities of high-variance trajectories does not straightforwardly imply a uniform lower bound over all feature directions without additional covering or design arguments. The sketch omits key steps needed for this implication.

The proof sketch for HYRULE contains dimension/horizon terms such as d^4H^8 and \beta d^7H^5 before concluding an H^3-leading regret rate. Without the full derivation, it is unclear whether these terms are genuinely lower order under the stated sample assumptions or whether they materially affect the bound. The presentation does not make this mathematically transparent.

The empirical methodology does not faithfully test the proposed algorithms: the paper explicitly substitutes LSVI-UCB for FORCE inside OPTCOV and LinPEVI-ADV for LinPEVI-ADV+, and uses LSVI-UCB++ 'as-is' for Algorithm 2. Therefore the experiments are not direct validations of RAPPEL/HYRULE as theoretically analyzed.

The paper includes a footnote asserting a typo in He et al. (2023) and modifies a variance clipping term from H to \sqrt{H}. While the argument may be plausible, changing a key component of a baseline/theoretical primitive requires especially careful re-verification. From the provided text, it is not fully clear that all downstream guarantees remain valid under this modification.

There is an inconsistency between strong practical claims and the evidence provided. The text mentions testing on a 'complex real-world healthcare dataset' and challenges in generalization, but the actual experiments shown are only on scaled-down Tetris. This discrepancy undermines empirical validity and suggests possible leftover or unsupported claims in the manuscript.
